rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all eight compounds and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.
Double the gradient duration with all other settings fixed to reveal which crowded pairs respond to slope. This should spread the central cluster and late pair while keeping all compounds observable.
Keep the shallower slope and raise temperature to test selectivity of the remaining close pair. Higher temperature should also reduce the small time penalty.
Step down from 60 C to separate the newly coeluting pair while largely preserving the improved central-cluster selectivity. Keeping the gradient fixed isolates this temperature effect.

At 60 C, slightly steepen the gradient to move the coeluting pair apart through slope-dependent selectivity. The other pairs had resolution margin at this temperature, and the shorter gradient should keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

The formerly coeluting pair improved when the gradient was shortened, so continue to 18 minutes to target baseline separation. This tests whether that gain outweighs compression of the neighboring pairs while retaining ample margin below the time limit.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to fine-tune selectivity while slightly reducing gradient steepness. This targets the sole marginal pair at R = 1.46, with the first peak still sufficiently retained to permit this adjustment.

Use a narrower gradient window to access a slope of 0.045 organic fraction per minute, between the tested slopes near the optimum. This should lift the two marginal central resolutions while preserving separation of the later pair, with all peaks expected to elute within the gradient.

Injection 8 already achieves the maximum CRF; retain it as the benchmark. Test a higher starting organic fraction with a slightly shallower slope to shorten the elution window while attempting to preserve baseline resolution of the three critical pairs.

The higher starting fraction sacrificed central-pair resolution, so restore the successful gradient window and probe a cooler selectivity regime. Injection 8 remains the maximum-score benchmark; this test may reveal another fully resolved region with more room for shortening.

Test the low-temperature endpoint to see whether temperature-dependent reordering separates the two close pairs observed at 35 C. Keep the gradient fixed to isolate selectivity changes, while retaining injection 8 as the maximum-score method.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving its slope to shorten the promising 25 C separation and test starting-composition selectivity of its one unresolved pair. Injection 8 remains the benchmark with the maximum CRF.

Test whether a further upward window shift carries the close central pair through an elution-order reversal into useful separation, while shortening retention. This is exploratory; injection 8 remains the established maximum-score method.

Shift the window upward one more step at the same slope to improve the central pair that separated as phi0 increased to 0.30. This could achieve full resolution in a substantially shorter elution window than injection 8.
Injection 14 achieves maximum CRF with a much shorter elution window. Shorten its gradient by one step to test whether all pairs remain above R = 1.5 as the last peak moves earlier.

Use an intermediate slope of 0.050 organic fraction per minute to recover the marginal pair from injection 15 while remaining faster than injection 14. The last peak should still elute within the gradient, with all pairs predicted to exceed R = 1.5.

Raise temperature one step from the fastest fully resolved method to seek earlier elution while testing whether its critical pairs retain baseline resolution. Injection 16 remains the shorter maximum-score benchmark if temperature compromises selectivity.

Return to 25 C and test a higher starting fraction at the same slope, seeking a faster separation beyond a possible central-pair elution-order reversal. Monitor early-peak compression carefully; injection 16 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test a warmer selectivity regime beyond the central-pair convergence seen at 30 C, while avoiding the early-peak compression caused by phi0 = 0.45. This may reveal a faster fully resolved separation; injection 16 remains the confirmed benchmark.

Return to 25 C and combine a one-step higher starting fraction with a shallower gradient to counter central-pair compression. This tests whether the last peak can elute earlier than in injection 16 while preserving full resolution.

Test a higher-starting-organic window at 60 C to look for a fast separation beyond the central-cluster order changes seen at intermediate temperature. Injection 16 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method, so this is an exploratory alternative.

Flatten the latest gradient while keeping its window and temperature fixed to test whether the two compressed early pairs gain sufficient resolution. The short retention window leaves room to improve separation while potentially remaining faster than injection 16.

Return near the successful low-temperature region and steepen the phi0 = 0.30 gradient to target its previously marginal central pair. This tests an alternative fully resolved method with potentially better central-pair margins, while retaining injection 16 as the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Raise the temperature one step on injection 23 to test whether its different starting composition permits faster elution without losing full resolution. Injection 16 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method if either marginal pair deteriorates.

Trim injection 16’s gradient endpoint while preserving its successful slope; all peaks are expected to elute before the gradient ends at the outlet at 4.65 minutes. This should retain maximum CRF and the approximately 4.14-minute last peak with a shorter programmed gradient.
